content.text:
The session stopped because of a bug in the runner, not because the agent decided to stop or a tool failed. A turn that runs past 60 minutes hits a timeout, and the runner then ends it as if it had finished normally.

The work itself was finished: [PR #7939](https://github.com/Agenta-AI/agenta/pull/7939) was open and the cleanup was done. The bug only removed the agent's final report. You got that report at 16:58, after you asked "what happened here?".

**What happened (all times UTC):**

| Time | Event |
|---|---|
| 14:21:38 | The runner sends the prompt to the agent. That HTTP request stays open for the whole turn. |
| 15:21:37 | The agent starts its last tool call, a Bash command that waits for CI. |
| 15:21:46 | The request hits the 60-minute limit and fails with `HeadersTimeoutError`. |
| 15:21:46 | The ACP client retries and sends the same prompt again. The transcript shows the identical text queued 180 ms after the failure. |
| 15:22:42.664 | The Bash command finishes. |
| 15:22:42.672 | Claude takes in the queued copy of the prompt (`absorbed_mid_turn`). |
| 15:22:42.674 | The adapter sees a new prompt and ends the first one with `end_turn`. |
| 15:22:42.837 | The runner treats this as a normal finish and removes the sandbox, so the agent never gets to reply. |

This also explains why the session looked successful: the execution shows `completed`, there is no error, and the turn has no final message or `usage` record.

**Where the bug is:**
- **Timeout:** the 60-minute limit is `DEFAULT_ACP_HEADERS_TIMEOUT_MS` in `services/runner/src/engines/sandbox_agent/acp-fetch.ts`. A long turn can hit it even when it is healthy, because the agent keeps working while that request stays open.
- **Retry:** our patch `services/runner/patches/acp-http-client@0.4.2.patch` treats this timeout as safe to retry, because the error text contains `fetch failed`. Resending a prompt is not safe, because the agent runs it as a new message.
- **Adapter:** `claude-agent-acp` ends the current turn when a queued prompt arrives, as designed, so the fix belongs in the runner.

**Who it affects:** any Claude turn on the runner that lasts longer than 60 minutes can stop this way. oss-team runs v0.127.1, and `release/v0.127.3` has the same timeout and retry code. The older oss-team logs show this timeout four more times on 2026-10-26 and 2026-10-27, but I did not check those sessions.

**The fix I recommend:** never retry the prompt request after it was sent, and remove the 60-minute limit on that request. The runner's own limits for stuck turns still apply.

**Separate problem:** the dev box disk is 99% full, with 29 GB free of 1.5 TB. This did not cause the stop, but it can break the stacks on this box if it fills up.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# Daily dev box cleanup. Removes only things that are provably safe to remove and
# reports everything it will not touch. Run by cron; see the log for what it did.
#
#   --dry-run   show what would be removed, change nothing
#
# Safety rules, in order. A worktree or directory is removed ONLY if all hold:
#   1. It is not the main checkout of its repository.
#   2. No running container mounts it and no process has it as a working directory.
#   3. It has no uncommitted changes.
#   4. Its HEAD commit is reachable from some remote branch, so nothing is lost.
#   5. Both its last commit and its directory are older than AGE_DAYS.
#
# Deployments and memory are REPORTED only. Removing a stack is a judgment call and
# stays with a person.

set -uo pipefail

AGE_DAYS=14
IMAGE_AGE_DAYS=7
LOG=/home/mahmoud/devbox-cleanup.log
REPOS=(
  /home/mahmoud/code/agenta-2
  /home/mahmoud/code/agenta
  /home/mahmoud/code/agenta_cloud
  /home/mahmoud/code/agenta-infra
)

DRY=no
[ "${1:-}" = "--dry-run" ] && DRY=yes

exec >> "$LOG" 2>&1
echo
echo "================ $(date '+%F %T')  dry-run=$DRY ================"

before_kb=$(df -k --output=avail / | tail -1)
cutoff=$(date -d "$AGE_DAYS days ago" +%s)
now=$(date +%s)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- in-use paths
# Any host path a running container mounts, plus any process working directory.
# Read once: both lists are needed for every candidate below.
inuse_file=$(mktemp)
trap 'rm -f "$inuse_file"' EXIT
{
  docker ps -q 2>/dev/null | xargs -r docker inspect \
    --format '{{range .Mounts}}{{.Source}}{{"\n"}}{{end}}' 2>/dev/null
  ls -l /proc/*/cwd 2>/dev/null | sed 's/.*-> //'
} | grep -E '^(/home/mahmoud|/tmp)/' | sort -u > "$inuse_file"

is_in_use() {  # $1 = path. True when the path, or anything under it, is in use.
  grep -q "^$1\(/\|$\)" "$inuse_file"
}

removed=0
kept_dirty=0
kept_unpushed=0
kept_inuse=0
kept_young=0

# ------------------------------------------------------------------- worktrees
echo "--- worktrees older than ${AGE_DAYS} days"
for repo in "${REPOS[@]}"; do
  [ -d "$repo/.git" ] || continue
  # The "is this commit on a remote" test below is only as good as the
  # remote-tracking refs. Refresh them first, and never block on a slow network.
  timeout 120 git -C "$repo" fetch --all --prune --quiet 2>/dev/null \
    || echo "  note: fetch failed for $repo; containment checks use cached refs"
  main=$(git -C "$repo" rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-common-dir 2>/dev/null | sed 's|/\.git$||')
  while read -r wt; do
    [ -n "$wt" ] || continue
    [ "$wt" = "$repo" ] && continue
    [ "$wt" = "$main" ] && continue
    [ -d "$wt" ] || continue

    if is_in_use "$wt"; then
      echo "  keep (in use)      $wt"; kept_inuse=$((kept_inuse+1)); continue
    fi

    commit_ts=$(git -C "$wt" log -1 --format=%ct 2>/dev/null || echo 0)
    dir_ts=$(stat -c %Y "$wt" 2>/dev/null || echo 0)
    newest=$(( commit_ts > dir_ts ? commit_ts : dir_ts ))
    if [ "$newest" -ge "$cutoff" ]; then
      kept_young=$((kept_young+1)); continue
    fi

    if [ -n "$(git -C "$wt" status --porcelain 2>/dev/null)" ]; then
      echo "  keep (uncommitted) $wt"; kept_dirty=$((kept_dirty+1)); continue
    fi

    # The decisive test. `git log @{u}..` reports nothing when a branch has no
    # upstream at all, which reads as "pushed" and is wrong. Ask instead whether
    # the commit itself lives on any remote branch.
    head_sha=$(git -C "$wt" rev-parse HEAD 2>/dev/null)
    if [ -z "$head_sha" ] || [ -z "$(git -C "$wt" branch -r --contains "$head_sha" 2>/dev/null | head -1)" ]; then
      echo "  keep (not on any remote) $wt"; kept_unpushed=$((kept_unpushed+1)); continue
    fi

    age_days=$(( (now - newest) / 86400 ))
    if [ "$DRY" = yes ]; then
      echo "  WOULD REMOVE (${age_days}d) $wt"
    elif git -C "$repo" worktree remove --force "$wt" 2>/dev/null; then
      echo "  removed (${age_days}d)     $wt"; removed=$((removed+1))
    else
      echo "  FAILED to remove   $wt"
    fi
  done < <(git -C "$repo" worktree list --porcelain 2>/dev/null | awk '/^worktree /{print $2}')
  [ "$DRY" = yes ] || git -C "$repo" worktree prune 2>/dev/null
done

# --------------------------------------------------- stray checkouts under /tmp
# Agent sessions leave full clones in /tmp. Apply the same five rules. A directory
# that is not a git repository is reported, never removed: its contents are unknown.
echo "--- stray /tmp checkouts older than ${AGE_DAYS} days"
for d in /tmp/agenta-* /tmp/opencode/*; do
  [ -d "$d" ] || continue
  is_in_use "$d" && continue
  dir_ts=$(stat -c %Y "$d" 2>/dev/null || echo 0)
  [ "$dir_ts" -ge "$cutoff" ] && continue
  if [ ! -e "$d/.git" ]; then
    # Report only the ones big enough to matter; the rest are scratch directories.
    sz=$(du -sm "$d" 2>/dev/null | cut -f1)
    [ "${sz:-0}" -ge 200 ] && echo "  keep (${sz} MB, not a git repo, review by hand) $d"
    continue
  fi
  # A /tmp clone can be a worktree of a repo above; those were handled already.
  git -C "$d" rev-parse --is-inside-work-tree >/dev/null 2>&1 || continue
  [ -n "$(git -C "$d" status --porcelain 2>/dev/null)" ] && { echo "  keep (uncommitted) $d"; kept_dirty=$((kept_dirty+1)); continue; }
  head_sha=$(git -C "$d" rev-parse HEAD 2>/dev/null)
  [ -z "$(git -C "$d" branch -r --contains "$head_sha" 2>/dev/null | head -1)" ] && { echo "  keep (not on any remote) $d"; kept_unpushed=$((kept_unpushed+1)); continue; }
  if [ "$DRY" = yes ]; then echo "  WOULD REMOVE $d"; else rm -rf "$d" && { echo "  removed $d"; removed=$((removed+1)); }; fi
done

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------- docker
echo "--- docker"
if [ "$DRY" = yes ]; then
  echo "  would remove exited containers older than ${AGE_DAYS} days:"
  docker ps -a -f status=exited --format '{{.Names}} {{.Status}}' 2>/dev/null | grep -Ei "days ago|weeks ago|months ago" | head -20 | sed 's/^/    /'
  echo "  would prune dangling images and build cache older than ${AGE_DAYS} days"
else
  docker container prune -f --filter "until=${AGE_DAYS}00h" 2>/dev/null | tail -1 | sed 's/^/  containers: /'
  docker image prune -f --filter "until=${AGE_DAYS}00h" 2>/dev/null | tail -1 | sed 's/^/  images:     /'
  docker builder prune -f --filter "until=${AGE_DAYS}00h" 2>/dev/null | tail -1 | sed 's/^/  cache:      /'
  # `image prune` without -a keeps every tagged image, so old runner and web
  # builds (4.6 GB each) pile up forever. -a removes any image no container,
  # running or stopped, references. A stopped stack still pins its images.
  docker image prune -a -f --filter "until=${IMAGE_AGE_DAYS}00h" 2>/dev/null | tail -1 | sed 's/^/  unused imgs:/'
fi

# ------------------------------------------------------------- package caches
# uv, pnpm and playwright keep every version ever downloaded. Pruning drops only
# what no environment or project references, so nothing installed breaks.
echo "--- package caches"
if [ "$DRY" = yes ]; then
  du -sh ~/.cache/uv ~/.local/share/pnpm/store ~/.cache/ms-playwright 2>/dev/null | sed 's/^/  /'
else
  uv cache prune -q 2>/dev/null && echo "  uv cache pruned"
  pnpm store prune 2>/dev/null | tail -1 | sed 's/^/  pnpm: /'
  npx --yes playwright uninstall --all >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "  playwright: removed browsers no project references"
fi

# Volumes need a stricter rule than `docker volume prune`. A stack that is merely
# stopped still owns its volumes, and pruning them destroys its database. Remove a
# volume only when its compose project has no containers left at all.
echo "--- docker volumes with no containers left"
dead_projects=$(mktemp); trap 'rm -f "$inuse_file" "$dead_projects"' EXIT
live_projects=$(docker ps -a --format '{{.Label "com.docker.compose.project"}}' 2>/dev/null | sort -u | grep -v '^$')
vol_removed=0
while read -r v; do
  [ -n "$v" ] || continue
  proj=$(docker volume inspect "$v" --format '{{index .Labels "com.docker.compose.project"}}' 2>/dev/null)
  [ -z "$proj" ] || [ "$proj" = "<no value>" ] && continue
  echo "$live_projects" | grep -qx "$proj" && continue
  if [ "$DRY" = yes ]; then
    echo "$proj" >> "$dead_projects"
  elif docker volume rm "$v" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    vol_removed=$((vol_removed+1)); echo "$proj" >> "$dead_projects"
  fi
done < <(docker volume ls -qf dangling=true 2>/dev/null)
if [ -s "$dead_projects" ]; then
  sort "$dead_projects" | uniq -c | while read -r n proj; do
    [ "$DRY" = yes ] && echo "  WOULD REMOVE $n volume(s) of $proj (stack no longer exists)" \
                     || echo "  removed $n volume(s) of $proj (stack no longer exists)"
  done
fi
[ "$DRY" = yes ] || echo "  removed $vol_removed volume(s) in total"

# ------------------------------------------------- deployments: report, not act
# Stopping a colleague's stack is never safe to automate. Name them and stop there.
echo "--- deployments idle for more than ${AGE_DAYS} days (REPORT ONLY, nothing stopped)"
docker ps -a --format '{{.Label "com.docker.compose.project"}}|{{.CreatedAt}}' 2>/dev/null \
  | awk -F'|' '$1!=""{ if ($2 > newest[$1]) newest[$1]=$2 } END { for (p in newest) print p, substr(newest[p],1,10) }' \
  | while read -r proj day; do
      age=$(( (now - $(date -d "$day" +%s 2>/dev/null || echo "$now")) / 86400 ))
      [ "$age" -gt "$AGE_DAYS" ] && echo "  $proj  idle ${age}d  (stop with: bash hosting/docker-compose/run.sh --down)"
    done

# Build router

This skill picks a workflow by the size and risk of the work, then runs it. Each workflow is a
short list of blocks, and each block is its own skill with its own gate. The workflow files are
in `workflows/` next to this file.

## Step 1: Pick the tier

Read the task, the linked issue, and the code it touches. Then go through the tiers from the
top, and take the first tier whose rules match. A task that matches any one rule of a tier goes
in that tier.

| Tier | Entry rules (any one is enough) | Workflow |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Program | More than three PRs. Mahmoud wants the work split into milestones that ship separately. | `workflows/program.md` |
| Feature | One to three PRs. A new contract (API, wire field, config shape, database table). A migration. It touches access checks, credentials, billing, or the runner. It needs a product decision from Mahmoud. | `workflows/feature.md` |
| Bug | Something that should work does not, and the fix is one PR. | `workflows/bug.md` |
| Small change | One PR, under about 300 changed lines, no new contract, no migration, and it does not touch access checks, credentials, billing, or the runner. | `workflows/small.md` |

A bug whose fix needs a new contract, a migration, or a product decision is a Feature. The
"risky areas" in every workflow are access checks, credentials, billing, the runner, and
migrations.

## Step 2: Tell Mahmoud the tier in one line

Send one line, then start the workflow without waiting for an answer:

```
Tier: Feature, because it adds a field to the secrets API. Say "make it a Program" to move it up.
```

Mahmoud can move a task up a tier at any time. Move a task down only when he says so. When the
work grows past its tier while you build (a second PR, a new contract, a risky area), move it up
yourself, tell him in one line, and run the blocks the higher tier adds.

## Step 3: Run the workflow

Open the workflow file for the tier and run its blocks in the listed order. Each block names the
skill that runs it and the gate it must pass. Do not start a block whose inputs depend on a gate
that has not passed. Blocks whose inputs are ready run at the same time.

## Rules for every tier

Roles:
- The orchestrator decides and delegates. Give each subagent one narrow job with full context:
  the goal, the files and symbols, the acceptance check, and the area `AGENTS.md`. A subagent
  that must guess produces work you redo.
- Subagents report up. A subagent never starts its own fixers for side bugs it finds. It lists
  them, and the orchestrator decides.
- Models: Opus for implementation, design and verification. Sonnet for QA driving, recordings,
  labels, status edits, and other mechanical steps. The `review-loop` skill picks the review
  models.

Building:
- Read the current code before you plan. Where the code differs from the issue or an old plan,
  the code is the truth.
- Make the smallest correct change at the root cause. Match the surrounding code. Do not
  refactor next door.
- Check the property at the system boundary that ships: the wire payload, the rendered page in
  `/m` (`web/mobile`, the main app), and Daytona for anything that runs in a cloud sandbox. A
  test that only runs the changed file shows the change, not the fix. When one policy has
  several readers, check every reader.
- When the work defines or changes an interface (API params, wire field, config schema, tool
  definition, event payload), run the `design-interfaces` skill on it.
- When the change moves an interface, endpoint, config field, default, or runtime behavior, run
  the `keep-docs-in-sync` skill in the same PR.
- Before each commit: `~/.local/bin/ruff format` then `~/.local/bin/ruff check --fix` in the API,
  SDK or services folder you touched (never `uvx ruff`), and `pnpm lint-fix` in `web/` for
  frontend changes.
- A sandbox image change (`services/runner/images/sandbox/**`, `agent-requirements.txt`, harness
  pins) bumps `services/runner/config/sandbox-recipe.json` in the same PR.
- No backward compatibility shims, no runtime flag injection, and no user-facing text you made
  up. Quote every new user-facing string in your report.

Branches and PRs:
- One PR in the GitButler workspace (`~/code/agenta`): a lane made with `but branch new <name>`,
  committed with `but commit <lane> --only`. Load the `gitbutler-stacks` skill for any stacked or
  multi-lane work. Take `but oplog snapshot -m "..."` before any risky `but` operation.
- Parallel work, or a busy workspace: a separate clone or worktree, as the `milestones` skill
  describes. Raw git is fine in your own clone.
- The PR base is the open release branch when one is open, else `main`. A stacked PR uses its
  parent branch. Open PRs ready for review, never as drafts.
- Never merge into `main`. A build agent does not merge into the release branch. The PR goes to
  the merge queue (`release-merge-queue`), unless Mahmoud gave release fix authority in this
  session.

Writing and decisions:
- Load `~/.claude/skills/plain-writing/SKILL.md` and `communicating-with-mahmoud` before you
  write any report, PR body, comment, artifact, or question. Repeat the reader profile and the
  banned patterns inline in every subagent brief that writes for Mahmoud.
- Put plans, open questions and reports for Mahmoud on an artifact page, with a short chat

- Start every GitHub comment with `🤖 _The AI agent says:_ `. Never sign as Claude.
- The agenta repo is public. No customer data, cloud host names, project ids, IPs, secrets, or
  local paths in a PR, commit, issue, or comment.

Loops:
- Cap every fix loop. When a round makes no progress, or after three rounds, stop. Then either

## Speed

Speed is a goal, and quality must not drop.
- Run independent blocks and agents at the same time. For example, start the QA agents while the
  review loops run, and rerun only the QA cells that the review fixes touch.
- Do not wait for a result the next step does not need. Open the PR as soon as the first slice

- Prefer small fast checks: the targeted test file before the full suite, one API call before a
  browser drive.

  gate passed. Do not run it again.
- Do not poll in a loop. Start a background wait and do other work.
- Merge first and fix forward only where the merge queue allows it (never for migrations, auth,

# Spec pages

The OpenSpec change is the core artifact of a Feature or a Program. The design review, the
milestones, the implementation, the reviews and the QA all work from it. The `build` router
calls this skill for the Feature and Program tiers. Bug and Small change tiers do not use it.

This skill makes three things:

1. The OpenSpec change in `openspec/changes/<name>/`.
2. A decision page: one card per open product question, each with an example conversation,
   the options, and a recommendation.
3. An OpenSpec viewer: the change rendered exactly as written, one tab per file.

Publish the decision page first, while product choices are open. Publish the viewer once the
spec is written and needs review.

## Writing rules for both pages

Load `~/.claude/skills/plain-writing/SKILL.md` and `~/.claude/skills/communicating-with-mahmoud/SKILL.md`
before you write. Then also follow these rules:

- For every behavior, show today (from the code, with `file:line` in the spec) next to the
  expected behavior.
- Every choice lists its options, the trade-off of each option, and one recommendation with
  the reason.
- The decision page has no code talk. The OpenSpec files may name files, functions and
  config shapes.
- Keep the design small. Before you propose machinery for a rare case, ask whether a narrower
  rule or a documented limit is enough. The `review-simplify` lens explains how to judge it.
- When the change defines or changes an interface (API route, request or response field,
  wire field, config schema, tool definition, event payload), load the `design-interfaces`
  skill and classify each field by its role before the spec is final.

## Step 1: Write the OpenSpec change

Read the code first. Every "today" statement needs evidence. Create
`openspec/changes/<name>/` with these files:

- `proposal.md`: `## Why`, `## What Changes`, `## Capabilities` (New and Modified), and
  `## Impact`.
- `design.md`: `## Context` (today's behavior, with evidence), `## Goals / Non-Goals`,
  `## Decisions` (each decision with a table of options and trade-offs, the chosen option in
  bold), then `## Risks / Trade-offs` and `## Migration`.
- `specs/<capability>/spec.md`: `## ADDED Requirements` (or `MODIFIED`). Under it,
  `### Requirement: <name>` with one sentence that uses SHALL, then one or more
  `#### Scenario: <name>` blocks with `- **WHEN** ...` and `- **THEN** ...` lines.
- `tasks.md`: numbered sections with `- [ ] 1.1 ...` checkboxes. Mark tasks that can run in
  parallel. For a Program, group tasks by milestone; the `milestones` skill splits them.

14	## 0. The prefilled template
15	
16	GitHub prefills every PR from `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md`, which asks for Summary, Testing, Demo, Checklist, and Contributor Resources. That is not what this repo's PRs look like. Replace the prefilled body with the structure in section 2.

18	Two parts of the template still apply:
19	
20	- **Demo.** UI changes need a capture from the real app running your branch. Never substitute a mock-up, a component harness, or a recreated screen. If you cannot run the app, say the demo is outstanding and why, rather than filling the space with something that proves nothing.

26	
27	The title states the actual change in plain words.
28	
29	- Use the conventional prefix the repo already uses, e.g. `[fix] <Title>`, `[feat] <Title>`, `[chore] <Title>`, `[docs] <Title>`.
30	- If the user gave you an issue id, suffix it: `[fix] <Title> [AGE-1234]`.
31	- Define the title as an active intent in present tense, e.g `[fix] Resolve broken evaluation links`.
32	- Keep it under ~70 characters. Detail goes in the body.
33	
34	Good vs bad:
35	
36	- Good: `[fix] Map OpenInference tool definitions into real tool objects`
37	- Bad: `fix(api) parse X into structured objects` (abstract, says nothing concrete)
38	- Bad: `Update tool handling` (vague, no symptom, no domain)
39	
40	## 2. Body structure
41	
42	Use this shape unless the change is truly trivial:
43	
44	```
45	## Context
46	<one or two sentences: the symptom a user or teammate would notice, then the root cause in plain words>
47	
48	## Changes
49	<plain-words explanation of the change, with a concrete before/after when a data shape, signature, or behavior changed>
50	
51	## Tests / notes
52	<short bullet list or prose: what you verified, anything reviewers should watch for>
53	
54	## What to QA
55	<only for user-visible changes: short steps for the manual tester, see section 7>
56	```
57	
58	Adapt the headings if the situation calls for it (e.g. a pure feature PR might use "What this adds" instead of "What was broken"). The order stays the same: the obeservation (symptom or user-visible change first or intent), then the changes, then verification and validation.

71	>

76	> ```
77	>

94	- Bullet lists that restate every changed file. The diff already shows that.
95	- Marketing words: "comprehensive", "robust", "seamlessly", "leverage", "powerful".
96	- Bullets that exist only to fill space. Prefer one clear sentence to three vague bullets.

98	## 5. Prose rules
99	
100	Apply these general writing rules:
101	
102	- **No em dashes.** Replace with a period and a new sentence, parentheses, or a semicolon. Absolute rule.
103	- Active voice.
104	- Short sentences by default. Longer ones only when they help the flow.
105	- Complete sentences. Snippets are fine when they keep things short and clear.
106	- Don't overuse bold or bullets. Use them when they aid quick reading. Otherwise prose.
107	- 11th-grade English, except for unavoidable technical terms.
108	
109	## 6. Tests / notes section
110	
111	Keep this section short and concrete. Useful contents:
112	
113	- What you ran locally (`pnpm test`, `pytest tests/...`, manual UI check on `/observability`).
114	- Anything reviewers should poke at (a known-fragile area, a follow-up not in this PR).
115	- Migration or rollout notes if relevant.
116	
117	Skip the section entirely if there is nothing real to say. A blank "Tests" heading is worse than no heading.
118	
119	## 7. What to QA section
120	
121	If the change is user-visible and a teammate will test it manually, add a "What to QA" section. Write it for a tester who knows the product and has context: skip the basics, point at the right screens, and state the expected result of every check.
122	
123	- One line per check: where to go, what to do, what they should see.
124	- Name the exact pages and flows. "Test the feature" is not a check.
125	- Include the regression to watch for: the thing this change is most likely to have broken.
126	- If a check needs setup (a seeded project, an older record, a feature flag), say so in the same line.
127	- Use simple, clear language. Same prose rules as section 5.
128	
129	Example:
130	
131	> ## What to QA
132	> - Create a new automatic evaluator, name it, save. The table shows your name with a v1 tag, not "default".
133	> - Edit it and commit a config change. The name stays, the version bumps to v2.
134	> - Regression: run a new evaluation. The variant chips still say "default", not the app name.
135	
136	Skip the section when nothing is user-visible (pure refactor, CI, docs). A reviewer-only change needs the Tests section, not this one.
137	
138	## 8. Reviewer's first-30-seconds test
139	
140	Before you finalize, read your own draft and ask:
141	
142	1. After 30 seconds, does a reviewer know **the context** and **what changed**?
143	2. Is there a concrete before/after anywhere a shape or behavior moved?
144	3. Did you delete every sentence that doesn't earn its place?
145	4. Did you scan for em dashes and marketing words?
146	
147	If any answer is no, edit before you push.
148	
149	## 9. Worked example
150	
151	A bad first draft:
152	
153	```
154	## Summary
155	- Updated the tool parsing logic to handle OpenInference traces
156	- Improved compatibility with the playground
157	- Added robust error handling for edge cases
158	
159	## Includes
160	- Modified parseTools function
161	- Updated type definitions
162	- Added new test cases
163	```
164	
165	A good rewrite:
166	
167	```
168	## Context
169	When you opened an OpenInference trace in the playground, the tools panel was empty. The trace stored tool definitions as `[{tool: {json_schema: "..."}}]`, but the playground expected the OpenAI shape `[{type: "function", function: {...}}]`, so the parser dropped them silently.
170	
171	## Changes
172	`parseToolsFromTrace` now unwraps `json_schema` and rebuilds each entry in the OpenAI shape before it hits the playground. Traces that already use the OpenAI shape pass through unchanged.
173	
174	Before:
175	[{tool: {json_schema: "{\"name\": \"get_weather\", ...}"}}]
176	
177	After:
178	[{type: "function", function: {name: "get_weather", parameters: {...}}}]
179	
180	## Tests
181	- Added a unit test in parseToolsFromTrace.test.ts covering both shapes.
182	- Opened a real OpenInference trace from the staging project and confirmed the tools panel renders.
183	
184	## What to QA
185	- Open an OpenInference trace in the playground (the staging project has them). The tools panel lists the tools.
186	- Regression: open a trace from the OpenAI SDK. The tools panel still renders as before.
187	```
188	
189	The second version is cleaner and tells the reviewer everything they need to start reading the diff.
